claims.text: Adding up to approximately 5 at.% noble-metal dopants promotes stable passivating surface-layer formation in near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles.
The passivating surface layers suppress high-temperature interdiffusion and phase segregation.
Noble-metal doping preserves nanoparticle structural and chemical integrity during repeated thermal cycling.
The proposed initial nanoparticle diameter is approximately 5–20 nm.
Noble-metal concentration will be systematically varied from 0 to approximately 5 at.%.
The controlled thermal history alternates catalytic steps at 773–1173 K with thermoelectric steps spanning 473–1923 K.
Testing will use an oxidizing or catalytic environment and at least 50 heating and cooling cycles.
Protective surface oxides become enriched in noble-metal species.
The proposed protective surface oxides reduce bulk element loss and retard phase separation or sintering.
Noble-metal dopants preferentially concentrate at the nanoparticle surface.
Thin, stable surface oxide layers act as diffusion barriers.
Reducing atomic diffusion can kinetically restrain phase separation or precipitate formation.
Limiting outward diffusion confines less stable elements within the nanoparticles and preserves single-phase chemical homogeneity.
Nanoparticles containing approximately 5 at.% noble metal will show less sintering than undoped controls after at least 50 cycles.
Nanoparticles containing approximately 5 at.% noble metal will show less compositional drift and greater single-phase retention than undoped controls.
Undoped nanoparticles are expected to undergo accelerated coarsening, phase separation, or surface segregation under the same thermal history.
Noble-metal contents above approximately 5 at.% may reduce the proposed stability advantage.
Strongly reducing environments may limit passivation and therefore reduce the proposed stability advantage.
Above the proposed composition or environmental boundaries, internal oxidation or multiphase precipitation may become operative.
Comparable stability of undoped and approximately 5 at.% noble-metal-doped nanoparticles, or failure of doping to mitigate decomposition, would falsify the hypothesis.
